What's your go to way to get a discount on something.
Pirating it is usually a good start.
Until 3D printing everything becomes a viable option I still have to buy some physical goods.
Retailmenot.com , googling for discount codes, asking .... usually in that order

This reminds me of another option. Sign up for sites like FatWallet or eBates (I find that sometimes one has a better discount than the other on a particular store). Be sure to click through the site you plan to purchase from from FatWallet/eBates, and you could get a decent chunk of cash back. I forget to use them sometimes, but I've gotten around $1000 cash back between the two sites over the last few years on stuff I needed anyway.

Pointing out that a competitor is offering it for less.

Depending on the item, sometimes I'll also call out features that I don't need (particularly if they're "optional" features that normally you'd pay more for, but that I don't really want -- like when buying a car) and either ask them to remove them, or cut the cost of those features.

Also checking if they have any discounts for things you're affiliated with -- AAA, through your employer, military/veteran, local's discount (e.g. some places will give a discount if you live in a certain area they want to market more to), student discounts, senior citizen discounts, etc. You can ask the vendor directly, or sometimes find that info on their website.

Another tactic is to offer to buy more if they provide a discount. So, you may suggest that if they provide a discount of $X, you'll purchase twice as much (obviously this is only a good deal if you actually want/need more). This works great at places like a farmer's market or flea market where perhaps you're about to buy $11 worth of goods, but you might ask "Will you take $10 for it?"

Also check if places will provide a discount for paying in cash. Credit card fees eat into a merchant's profits. Depending on the merchant, they may be willing to share some of that with you provided you pay cash.

And then there's good old relationship building. If it's a merchant you frequent, start building a relationship. Talk to the people who work there/own the business, and get to know them. Be kind to them. Throw business their way (and let them know "hey, I was just telling my coworker about your amazing widgets! Do you guys have any in stock? He was thinking of coming by tomorrow.") And don't follow up every interaction with your hand out. But, I've found that by building relationships with certain merchants, they've given me unsolicited perks, freebies, discounts, etc. Or, when I've asked for a little compromise on price or something, they're far more likely to agree. Businesses are nothing without customers -- particularly quality, repeat customers. And a good merchant is going to want to keep it that way with you.

Oh, and ALWAYS act like you don't really need it, and never be afraid to walk away. Unless it's something that only that vendor can possibly offer, chances are you can find it somewhere else and negotiate a deal on it. Or purely by the act of walking away the merchant will realize that a lost sale is worse for their bottom line than a discounted sale, and may change their tune.

When you iron a beadsprite while it's on a pegboard, the heat from the iron tends to heat and warp the pegboard, much like it does to the beadsprite itself. In order to prevent this, you can use the "Masking Tape Method" to safely remove the beadsprite from the pegboard before ironing. This method is also useful if you have a beadsprite that uses more pegboards than you have available. You'll be able to build the entire beadsprite in pieces, then put them together before ironing.

Once your the beadsprite is built and ready for ironing, follow the steps below to remove it from the pegboard:

  1. Cover your completed beadsprite with strips of masking tape. Be sure to overlap each strip slightly and press down nice and firm, so it all sticks together.
  2. Poke holes through the masking tape inside of each bead. This is a very important step as it prevents heat from building up inside each bead as you iron. You only want the end of a bead to melt, not the whole bead!
  3. Remove the beadsprite from the pegboard(s) to another surface, masking tape side down.
  4. Iron the beadsprite.
  5. Once the beadsprite has cooled, flip it over and remove each strip of masking tape. Be careful when doing this as it may be possible to pull the beadsprite apart if you are a little too rough and it's not ironed thoroughly enough.

Here is an excellent video demonstration (not mine) showing most of the masking tape method. The only part this video doesn't cover is poking holes in the tape, but you can find several other videos demonstrating that if you search youtube for "masking tape method".

Here are a few tips to make things a little easier/quicker and help prevent you from messing up your design before ironing:

  • When putting on the masking tape, be especially careful not to let any of it touch the beads before it's positioned exactly where you want it. Once the tape touches a bead, it's going to be a huge hassle to reposition it. To help with this, try to keep the tape relatively taught (enough so it doesn't sag, but not so much that it stretches) and slowly lower it over the beadsprite until it's directly over top of where you want it stuck.
  • To speed up the hole poking, I've found that an extra pegboard works quite well. Simply position it upside-down along one edge of the beadsprite lining up the pegs with a row or two of beads. Press down until the pegs pierce the tape. This can take a good amount of force if you are using a thicker tape or if you overlapped the strips too much, but you can make it a little easier if you try to pierce the tape from one end of the row to the other. Once the tape is pierced for one row, move the extra pegboard to the next row in and do the same thing, continuing this process until the entire beadsprite is done. Make sure to open a hole for every bead, but don't worry about whether or not you poke any extra holes outside of the beadsprite; it doesn't hurt or help either way.
  • If you plan on making one side of the beadsprite ironed and one side unironed, be aware that you may need to flip the original design you're working from. When using the masking tape method, the side you see on the pegboard will be the unironed side. If you forget to flip it, you may be able to place a second set of pegboards on top (make sure the pegs go into the holes of the beads) and flip the whole thing over before adding the masking tape. This will be tricky with large sprites however.
  • For single pegboard beadsprites, you can usually just flip the whole thing quickly onto another surface to remove it from the pegboard. For multi-pegboard pieces, you can usually peel the beadsprites up off the pegboards using the masking tape, but you'll need to make especially certain the tape is well stuck to every bead.
  • When removing a strip of masking tape, I usually try to hold the beadsprite down along the edge of the tape and peel the tape slowly and as close to parallel as possible to the beadsprite.
